title: Chinese literature
wiki_lead: The history of Chinese literature extends thousands of years, and begins with the earliest recorded inscriptions, court archives, building to the major works of philosophy and history written during the Axial Age. The Han (202 BC – 220 AD) and Tang (618–907 AD) dynasties were considered golden ages of poetry, while the Song (960–1279) and Yuan (1271–1368) were notable for their lyrics (ci), essays, dramas, and plays. During the Ming and Qing, mature novels were written in written vernacular Chinese, an evolution from the preeminence of Literary Chinese patterned off the language of the Chinese classics. The introduction of widespread woodblock printing during the Tang and the invention of movable type printing by Bi Sheng (990–1051) during the Song rapidly spread written knowledge throughout China. Around the turn of the 20th century, the author Lu Xun (1881–1936) is considered an influential voice of vernacular Chinese literature.
grok_lead: Chinese literature constitutes one of the world's oldest and most extensive literary traditions, originating with oracle bone inscriptions from the late Shang dynasty around 1200 BCE and evolving continuously through dynastic eras into the present. It encompasses diverse genres including poetry, philosophical treatises, historical annals, and prose fiction, predominantly composed in Classical Chineseâa compact, non-colloquial languageâuntil the vernacular baihua movement in the early 20th century shifted toward modern spoken forms. Influenced heavily by Confucianism, which emphasized moral instruction and social harmony, the literature prioritizes ethical reflection, historical veracity, and aesthetic precision over individualistic romanticism prevalent in Western counterparts. The tradition's classical phase, spanning from the Zhou dynasty's Shijing anthology to the Tang dynasty's poetic zenith with figures like Li Bai and Du Fu, produced canonical works that integrated cosmology, governance, and human emotion, often under imperial patronage or scholarly examination systems. Ming and Qing eras marked the novel's ascendancy, yielding masterpieces such as Dream of the Red Chamber and the "Four Great Classical Novels," which critiqued societal decay through intricate narratives of family, adventure, and bureaucracy. Modern literature, catalyzed by the May Fourth Movement, adopted Western realism and vernacular expression to address nationalism and reform, with authors like Lu Xun exposing spiritual torpor in semi-colonial China. In the People's Republic era, state censorship under the Chinese Communist Party has constrained literary output, mandating alignment with party ideology and suppressing depictions of events like the Great Leap Forward famines or Tiananmen Square protests, thereby prioritizing propaganda over empirical realism and fostering self-censorship among writers. This contrasts sharply with pre-modern freedoms, where literati could subtly dissent via allegory, highlighting a causal shift from meritocratic bureaucracy to totalitarian control that has diminished the tradition's candid social critique.
